Thomas Jefferson. Born in 1743, died in 1826. The primary architect of American political philosophy and the nation's third president, but most remembered as the author of the Declaration of Independence. A Virginia planter, Enlightenment polymath, and champion of agrarian democracy, he shaped the young republic's foreign policy as Secretary of State and later doubled the nation's territory through the Louisiana Purchase as president. His tenure marked the triumph of republican ideals and westward expansion, though he left unresolved the profound contradiction between his democratic vision and his ownership of enslaved people.

Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence in 1776, articulating the revolutionary philosophy that all men are created with inalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. He grounded the Declaration in Enlightenment thought and popular sovereignty, replacing divine right with the consent of the governed as the sole basis of legitimate government. He served as Secretary of State under George Washington from 1790 to 1793, establishing the diplomatic protocols and foreign policy stance of the early republic.

Jefferson was elected president in 1800, defeating Alexander Hamilton's Federalist faction and inaugurating an era of Republican dominance. One of his first great acts was negotiating the Louisiana Purchase in 1803 with France, doubling the nation's territory and securing the Mississippi River trade routes vital to western expansion. He commissioned the Lewis and Clark Expedition from 1804 to 1806 to explore and map these newly acquired western territories, laying American claim to the Pacific Northwest. He championed the Embargo Act in 1807 to punish British impressment of American sailors and violations of neutral maritime rights, though the policy proved economically disastrous.

Jefferson believed in the agrarian ideal—a nation of independent small farmers, not urban factories—as the moral foundation of republican virtue and self-governance. He opposed Alexander Hamilton's vision of a strong central bank and industrial economy, fearing that consolidated power would corrupt republican institutions. Late in life, he founded the University of Virginia, chartered in 1819, designing its curriculum and architecture to embody his educational and enlightened ideals.

Jefferson embodied the Age of Enlightenment's confidence that reason, education, and natural rights could transform human society. His vision of America as a republic of independent farmers spread across an ever-expanding continent became the dominant ideology of nineteenth-century westward expansion and popular democracy. Yet his legacy is irrevocably shadowed by his enslaved people—over six hundred during his lifetime—a contradiction he acknowledged but never resolved, exposing the limits of Enlightenment universalism in the hands of men bound to slave labour.

George Washington was the president he served as Secretary of State. James Madison was his closest political ally, Secretary of State successor, and ideological partner in founding Republican opposition to Federalism. Alexander Hamilton was his primary intellectual opponent on federal power, banking, and economic development. The Louisiana Purchase was his greatest diplomatic and territorial achievement, and the Lewis and Clark Expedition was his western exploration commission that opened American claims to the Pacific. His vision was rooted in Enlightenment thought, and he shaped the ideological foundations of the American Revolution itself. Yet the institution of slavery in America—which he owned but philosophically condemned—marked the gap between his ideals and his actions.
